792.title: The suffering servant (Isaiah 53)
792.hook: Jewish tradition reads the servant as the people Israel in exile
792.howItsDone: Jews read Isaiah 52 and 53 as part of the book of Isaiah; Jewish commentators read the servant as the people Israel, and the passage is part of the conversation between Jews and Christians, who read it differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a city said she'd been forgotten, and heard: I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands. Your line was I will not forget thee. Did you reach the person you remembered? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

Somebody in this chapter is speaking, and they sound stunned. Kings shut their mouths. A voice asks, Who hath believed our report? And then a group starts to confess. We looked at him and saw nothing worth seeing. We turned our faces away. We thought he was struck down by God. But he was wounded for what we had done. Isaiah fifty-three is written mostly in the voice of onlookers, people realizing too late what they had done to someone they despised. The big question the chapter leaves is: who is the someone? And who are we?
screen: `KINGS SHUT THEIR MOUTHS.` → `A GROUP STARTS TO CONFESS.` → `WHO IS HE? WHO ARE WE?`

segments.voice: The onlookers describe him: "He was despised, and forsaken of men, A man of pains, and acquainted with disease." Wounded, bruised, led like a lamb, cut off, and yet in the end, the chapter says, he shall see his seed and prolong his days. So who is this servant? Jewish tradition answers from inside the book of Isaiah itself. A few chapters earlier, the prophet names the servant outright: "Thou art My servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified." And again: But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen. Read that way, the servant in chapter fifty-three is the people Israel in exile: scattered, mocked, treated as if their suffering proved God had abandoned them. And the we who are speaking are the nations, the kings who shut their mouths, finally seeing that the people they scorned carried more than their own share. Some Jewish readers hear the righteous within Israel, or the prophet himself, and the ancient Aramaic translation, the Targum, reads the passage's opening verse as speaking of the Messiah. Christians read this chapter as speaking of Jesus. The same words, read in different ways by two traditions, each with its own teachers and commentaries. On this path, we're following the Jewish reading. And notice what that reading does. It refuses the onlookers' first conclusion: he must have deserved it. The chapter turns that around. Suffering is not proof of guilt. A people can be despised and still be God's servant. Still be held. Still have a future.
screen: `A MAN OF PAINS, ACQUAINTED WITH DISEASE.` · `THOU ART MY SERVANT, ISRAEL.` · `THE ONLOOKERS ARE THE NATIONS.` · `SUFFERING IS NOT PROOF OF GUILT.` · then, large: `THE SERVANT IS THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with suffering that isn't deserved. Settle, and breathe. Let one person or one people come to mind who are suffering, and who are blamed for it. The ones people say must have brought it on themselves. Notice if any part of you has quietly agreed. Don't argue with it. Just set it down. Then stay with them for a while, the way the onlookers in the chapter finally did, looking instead of turning away. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The suffering servant. Isaiah fifty-three's despised and wounded figure, read in Jewish tradition as the people Israel in exile. Today's word.

Your line: the servant is the people. Today, when you hear someone's suffering explained as their own fault, pause before agreeing. Look again, the way the onlookers did. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

793.title: The fast I have chosen (Isaiah 58:6–7)
793.hook: read on Yom Kippur: loose the bonds, share your bread, house the poor
793.howItsDone: Isaiah 58 is read as the prophetic reading on Yom Kippur morning, and some Jews mark the day by giving charity or bringing food for those in need as the fast ends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the suffering servant, despised by onlookers who later saw they were wrong. Your line was the servant is the people. Did you look again before blaming someone? Day seven hundred ninety-three.

It's the morning of Yom Kippur. The synagogue is full of people who haven't eaten since the evening before. No food, no water, hours of prayer. And in the middle of it, someone stands up to read from the prophets, and the reading is Isaiah fifty-eight, in which God asks, more or less: is this the fast I want? On the fast day itself, the fasting people hear a prophet question their fasting. Some readers think that placement is the whole point.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR MORNING. NO FOOD, NO WATER.` → `THE READING: ISAIAH 58.` → `IS THIS THE FAST I WANT?`

segments.voice: The chapter starts with the people's complaint: "Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not?" We did everything right. Why isn't God noticing? And the prophet answers: on the day of your fast you still chase your own business and push your workers hard. You fast and quarrel. Then comes the turn: "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?" What the prophet does not say matters. He doesn't say: stop fasting. Yom Kippur is still a fast, and the people reading this chapter are still hungry while they read it. He says the fast was never only about the empty stomach. An empty stomach is meant to point somewhere: to the person whose stomach is empty without choosing it. Loose the bands. Undo the burdens. Share the bread. Open the house. And that last phrase: hide not thyself from thine own flesh. Don't look away from another human being, as if they weren't your own family. The fast and the bread belong together. Going hungry for a day, the chapter suggests, is meant to make a person notice the people who are hungry every day.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed someone hungry. Settle, and breathe. Notice your own stomach for a moment, full, empty or somewhere in between. Then let your mind go outward, to who near you might be hungry today. A neighbor. A shelter. A food bank on your way home. A coworker who skips lunch. Choose one concrete way to share bread this week: a meal, a donation, a bag of groceries, an extra plate at your table. If you pray, you can hold the verse: is not this the fast that I have chosen? The bell holds the time.

794.title: Call the Sabbath a delight (Isaiah 58:13)
794.hook: honor Shabbat by setting your own business aside
794.howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat set work and weekday business aside from Friday sundown to Saturday night, marking the day with candles, festive meals, prayer, rest and study; oneg Shabbat, the delight of the Sabbath, is a phrase drawn from this verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fast I have chosen: loose the bonds, open the house. Your line was share thy bread. Who did you share it with? Today, the same chapter, a few verses on. Day seven hundred ninety-four.

Friday night, after services, in some synagogues there's a table in the back: cake, tea, fruit, people lingering and talking. It may be called an oneg. A long table of sugar named after a verse of Isaiah. Oneg is the Hebrew word for delight, and it comes from the end of chapter fifty-eight, the same chapter that challenged the fasting people yesterday. Having asked for justice alongside the fast, the prophet turns to the seventh day, and he doesn't describe it as a duty or a burden. He says: call it a delight.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT: AN ONEG.` → `ONEG MEANS DELIGHT.` → `SAME CHAPTER AS YESTERDAY.`

segments.voice: The verse, near the chapter's end: "If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable." And it goes on: not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words. At first that sounds like a contradiction. Don't do your own pleasure, and call it a delight? But the Hebrew word the King James gives as pleasure can also mean business, your affairs, the things you're chasing. The 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders it thy business. So the picture becomes clearer. Turn your foot away. Step off the road you walk every weekday. Set down what you're pursuing. And in the space that leaves, find delight. The rabbis took even the last phrase seriously: speaking thine own words. In the Talmud, it's read as a guide to Shabbat talk. Don't spend the day talking about deals and errands and the to-do list. Let the conversation rest too. And the verb is call. Call the Sabbath a delight. It's something you name, and naming it changes how it's lived. The same hours can be named a day where nothing gets done, or a day of delight. And the promise at the end: then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord. The delight people give the day comes back to them. For Jews who keep it, that can mean candles, a good meal, a nap, a walk, a long talk at the table.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: delight in one hour of rest. Settle, and breathe. Look ahead at the next few days and find one hour you can give back. No business, no errands, no to-do list. Then ask: what would make that hour a delight, not just a gap? A walk. A meal with someone. A book. A nap. Music. Choose it now, and put it somewhere you'll see it. If you keep Shabbat, you can bring one new delight to it this week. The bell holds the time.

795.title: Arise, shine (Isaiah 60:1)
795.hook: "Arise, shine, for thy light is come"
795.howItsDone: Isaiah 60 is among the prophetic readings of comfort after Tisha B'Av, and its opening words, kumi ori, are sung on Friday nights in the Shabbat song Lecha Dodi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, oneg: set your business aside and call the Sabbath a delight. Your line was call it a delight. Did you guard your hour? Today, a line Shabbat sings. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

Wake up, wake up, for your light has come. That line is sung on Friday night in Lecha Dodi, the song that welcomes Shabbat like a bride, in a verse that calls out to a city. Inside it sit two Hebrew words: kumi ori. Arise, shine. They weren't written for the song. The poet borrowed them from Isaiah, from the opening of chapter sixty, where the prophet calls out to a city sitting in the dark.
screen: `WAKE UP, WAKE UP.` → `FRIDAY NIGHT: LECHA DODI.` → `KUMI ORI, BORROWED FROM ISAIAH.`

segments.voice: Chapter sixty opens: "Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee." The one being spoken to is Zion, the city, pictured as a woman. A few chapters earlier, Isaiah told her to shake herself from the dust. Now she's told to stand up. And look at the tense. Thy light is come. Not will come. Not might come if you try hard enough. It has come. The command to rise arrives after the light, not before it. She isn't told to make the morning. She's told to get up into a morning that's already here. And the very next verse is honest about the world around her: darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the people. The verse doesn't pretend the night is over everywhere. It says the light is on her, in the middle of that darkness, and that others will come toward it: nations shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising. And the order matters. Arise comes first, and shine comes second. You can't shine lying down. The first act is simply standing up. That's why the line fits a Friday night so well. The week may have been dark and heavy. The world may still be dark and heavy. But Shabbat has come in, and the song says: get up. Your light is here.
screen: `SPOKEN TO ZION, IN THE DUST.` · `THY LIGHT IS COME, ALREADY.` · `DARKNESS STILL COVERS THE EARTH.` · `FIRST STAND UP, THEN SHINE.` · then, large: `ARISE, SHINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin today brightly. Settle, and breathe. If you can, sit up a little taller, or stand. Let one thing that's already good in this day come to mind: light through a window, coffee, a person, a small piece of good news. It's here already; you don't have to earn it. Let it land. Then choose how you'll rise into the day: the first thing you'll do, and the face you'll bring to it. If you pray, you can hold the verse: arise, shine, for thy light is come. The bell holds the time.
Arise. In Hebrew, kumi, the first word of Isaiah sixty: arise, shine, for thy light is come. Today's word.
Your line: arise, shine. Today, when the day pulls you down, stand up first, literally, then get on with it. The light came before you did. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

796.title: A new earth (Isaiah 65:17–25)
796.hook: a vision of no weeping, houses built and lived in, the wolf and lamb at peace
796.tomorrow: Say not, I am a child (Jeremiah 1:4–10)
796.howItsDone: Jews read Isaiah's visions of a repaired world as part of the prophets, and some connect them with tikkun olam, the work of repairing the world through justice and kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kumi ori: stand up into a light that has already come. Your line was arise, shine. Did you stand up first? Today, our last day in Isaiah. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

A house with someone living in it who also built it. A vineyard where the person who planted the vines gets to drink the wine. A baby who grows up. An old man who lives out all his days. Children who stay with their parents. That's the list. Near the end of Isaiah, the prophet describes a whole new creation, and it turns out to look like an ordinary street on a good afternoon. No golden throne room, no clouds. Just the plain, unbroken things that war and exile kept taking away.
screen: `A HOUSE, BUILT AND LIVED IN.` → `A VINEYARD, PLANTED AND ENJOYED.` → `AN ORDINARY STREET, UNBROKEN.`

segments.voice: It opens big: "For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind." Then, almost at once, it comes down to street level. Jerusalem will be a joy, and the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her, nor the voice of crying. And here's the heart of it: "And they shall build houses, and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them." The next verse says it the other way around: they shall not build, and another inhabit; they shall not plant, and another eat. For a people who had watched their houses taken and their fields stripped, that is what a new earth means. Not escape from the world. The world, with the theft taken out of it. Your work stays yours. Your children grow up. Nobody's harvest goes to someone else. Then the vision reaches back to an earlier picture in Isaiah, the one from ten days ago: the wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock. And it ends: they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain. That's where our long walk through Isaiah closes, on a promise made of ordinary things. Some Jews speak of tikkun olam, repairing the world, as part of the work of moving toward a vision like this one. Different communities hold different hopes for how and when it comes. The text itself keeps it plain: a house, a vine, a long life, and no one hurting anyone on the mountain.
screen: `NEW HEAVENS AND A NEW EARTH.` · `NO MORE THE VOICE OF WEEPING.` · `BUILD HOUSES, AND INHABIT THEM.` · `THEY SHALL NOT HURT NOR DESTROY.` · then, large: `A NEW EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture one repaired corner of the world. Settle, and breathe. Choose one small place you know well: your street, your building, a school, a hospital ward, a park. Now let it be mended in your mind. Who lives there safely? Who gets to keep what they built? Who stops crying? See it clearly, in plain detail. Then notice one thing, however small, that you could do this week to move that corner a step closer. If you pray, you can hold the verse: they shall not hurt nor destroy. The bell holds the time.
A new earth. Isaiah sixty-five: houses built and lived in, vineyards planted and enjoyed, no more the voice of weeping. Today's word.
Your line: a new earth. Today, do one small thing for the corner you pictured, and let it be ordinary. Tomorrow, a new prophet, and a young one. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

797.title: Say not, I am a child (Jeremiah 1:4–10)
797.hook: the young prophet protests, and God touches his mouth
797.carry: say not, I am a child
797.howItsDone: Jeremiah's call is read in synagogue as a haftarah, the reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah reading, in the summer weeks before Tisha b'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah closed on a wolf and a lamb feeding together. Your line was a new earth. Did you do your one small thing? Today the scroll of Isaiah rolls shut, and a new prophet begins: Jeremiah. Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

The book of Jeremiah opens with a call, and the first thing the prophet does is say no. The word of the Lord comes to him: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee." Before you were born, I set you apart and made you a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah's answer comes straight back. "Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child." Wrong person, too young, no words. Moses, at the burning bush, made a similar case: I'm slow of speech. Today, what God says back to Jeremiah, and where his hand lands.
screen: `BEFORE I FORMED THEE, I KNEW THEE.` → `I CANNOT SPEAK.` → `FOR I AM A CHILD.`

segments.voice: The answer begins with the two words that give us today's word. "Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak." The Hebrew word Jeremiah uses for himself is na'ar, a word that can mean a boy, a youth, a young man. The text never tells us his age, and readers have guessed in different directions. What the story cares about is how he sees himself: too small for this. Now notice what God doesn't do. He doesn't argue that Jeremiah is older than he thinks, or more gifted, or more ready. There's no flattery at all. Instead, the weight moves somewhere else. You'll go where I send you. You'll say what I give you. And then: "Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee." Then the call turns physical. The Lord puts out his hand and touches Jeremiah's mouth, and says, "Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth." Jeremiah named his problem as his mouth, I cannot speak, and that's exactly where the touch lands. The call closes with a list of verbs: to root out and to pull down, to destroy and to throw down, to build and to plant. Most of them are about tearing down, and Jeremiah's book will have plenty of that. But the list ends on building and planting. So say not, I am a child, isn't a promise that he'll stop feeling small. It's permission to speak anyway, because the words were never supposed to come from his size.
screen: `SAY NOT, I AM A CHILD.` · `NA'AR: A BOY, A YOUTH.` · then, large: `I HAVE PUT MY WORDS IN THY MOUTH.` · then: `TO BUILD AND TO PLANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak up, even if you feel young. Settle, and breathe. Is there a room where you tend to go quiet? A meeting, a family table, a group where everyone else seems older or surer. Bring it to mind. Now find the one thing you would say there if size didn't matter: a question, a fact, a disagreement, a thank-you. Say it once to yourself, plainly, in your head. Then choose the moment this week when you'll say it out loud. If you pray, you can hold the words God said to Jeremiah: say not, I am a child. The bell holds the time.
Say not. God's answer to a prophet who called himself a child: the call isn't measured by your size. Today's word.
Your line: say not, I am a child. Today, say the one thing you usually leave to someone older or surer. Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

798.title: The watching tree (Jeremiah 1:11–12)
798.hook: an almond branch, shaked, sounds like "watching": God watches over the word
798.howItsDone: Jews read the almond-branch vision as part of Jeremiah's opening chapter, which is read in synagogue as a haftarah in the summer weeks before Tisha b'Av; Hebrew readers hear the shaked and shoked wordplay directly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prophet said he couldn't speak, and God touched his mouth. Your line was say not, I am a child. Did you say the thing? Today, Jeremiah's first vision, and it's a branch. Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

The next scene opens on a question, the kind a teacher asks: "Jeremiah, what seest thou?" No fire, no throne, no angels with wings. Jeremiah looks, and answers with something you could pick up on a hillside. "I see a rod of an almond tree." A stick. A branch from a tree. And God says: you have seen well. The vision is so ordinary that it needs the Hebrew to open it, and inside the Hebrew is a play on words, a serious one.
screen: `WHAT SEEST THOU?` → `A ROD OF AN ALMOND TREE.` → `YOU HAVE SEEN WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the play. The Hebrew word for almond is shaked. And God's answer, in the next verse, uses a word that sounds almost the same: shoked, watching, keeping watch. You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it. Shaked, shoked. Almond, watching. In the Hebrew text the two words are written with the same letters; only the vowels differ. So the branch isn't a riddle about trees. It's a sound that carries a promise: the word I give you is not asleep. Some readers add a picture from nature: the almond blossoms early, as if it's awake before the other trees. That's a reader's image, not the verse's, but it fits. In English the play is harder to hear. The King James Version translates the verse "for I will hasten my word to perform it." In that English, the pun vanishes; other translations render the word as watching, which at least points back to it, though only the Hebrew lets you hear it. And notice what kind of vision this is. Jeremiah has just been told he'll speak hard words to nations. His first lesson isn't in speaking at all. It's in seeing: look at a plain branch closely enough, and it turns out to be saying something. The same question, what seest thou, comes again in the very next verse. Jeremiah's training starts with his eyes.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one small sign. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes rest on one plain thing near you: a cup, a plant, a window, a shoe by the door. Ask Jeremiah's question quietly: what do I see? Name it plainly first. Then look a little longer. Who made it, who uses it, what has it been through? Let it say one thing to you, however small. If nothing comes, that's fine; the looking is the practice. If you pray, you can hold the verse: I watch over my word. The bell holds the time.
The watching tree. An almond branch, shaked, that sounds like shoked, watching: God keeps watch over the word. Today's word.

Your line: the watching tree. Today, stop once at an ordinary thing and ask, what seest thou? And look back at this week: the servant is the people, share thy bread, call it a delight, arise, shine, a new earth, say not, I am a child, and the watching tree. Day seven hundred ninety-eight.
